lineages.name: Norman Cook (Fatboy Slim)
lineages.why: A self-described late adopter who learnt one tool thoroughly. He used a pair of Akai S950s and an Atari ST, with a TB-303 and SE-1 for synth lines, building tracks from drum loops, breaks and samples by repetition and layering. On 'Praise You' he sped up the source record and time-stretched the chopped vocal line by line in the S950.

lineages.name: Liam Howlett (The Prodigy)
lineages.why: He wrote on a Roland W-30, starting from obscure soul and funk vinyl that he twisted and contorted before adding his own synths. The breaks came from an SP-1200 and the distortion from a Korg Prophecy and guitar pedals. His records went from -14 to -8.6 LUFS between Experience and The Fat of the Land.

lineages.name: The Chemical Brothers
lineages.why: Tom Rowlands and Ed Simons built 'Block Rockin' Beats' at Orinoco Studios from Bernard Purdie's drums on 'Changes', a Schoolly D vocal hook and borrowed bass. It went to UK number one and won a Grammy for Best Rock Instrumental. London's Sunday Social club night was one of the genre's key rooms.

name: Breakbeat / big beat

notes.text: The drums are breaks: syncopated patterns cut from funk, jazz and R&B records. The most sampled are the Amen break, James Brown's 'Funky Drummer' (1970), the Incredible Bongo Band's 'Apache' (1973) and Lyn Collins' 'Think (About It)' (1972).

Big beat breaks are heavy, distorted and heavily compressed, in 'an arms race' for the chunkiest beats. Its hits sat around 90-120 BPM, faster than hip-hop and trip-hop but slower than house's 120 baseline; Wikipedia gives the genre 100-140 BPM overall.

The Akai S950 is a 12-bit sampler, and Fatboy Slim works almost entirely on a pair of them. He refused to upgrade because he knew the S950's filters so well, and its timestretch (added in 1988) lets length and pitch change independently.

Liam Howlett sketched The Fat of the Land on a Roland W-30, used an E-mu SP-1200 for the 'Firestarter' breaks, and got the distortion from a Korg Prophecy, Boss guitar pedals and an Alesis Quadraverb. He mixed in Cubase on a Power Mac.
Roland TB-303 acid lines from acid house, or bass lifted from records: the bass sound on 'Block Rockin' Beats' comes from The Crusaders, and its line is allegedly from 23 Skidoo.

Not harmony-driven: one to three chord modal loops under the break, for example Mixolydian bVII-IV-I on 'Praise You' and Dorian i-IV on 'Right Here Right Now'. Riffs and samples carry the interest, not the changes.

Tracks are collages of many samples: 'Praise You' uses nine, including a Camille Yarbrough vocal, a Hoyt Axton piano and drums from three different records. Norman Cook sped up the record, chopped the vocal into short pieces and time-stretched each line in the S950.

The form is built from crescendos, builds, drops and extended drum rolls, and moved along with filters, phasers and flangers. It is looser than DJ-tool genres, and track lengths run from about 4:40 to 7 minutes.

evidence.inferred: No cited source gives bar counts for big beat sections; the plan divides Block Rockin' Beats (5:14 at 109 BPM, about 143 bars) and Praise You (5:23 at 110 BPM, about 148 bars) into 16-bar units

notes.text: Forms vary a lot; the section plan in this profile is an assumption sized to the reference lengths, not a documented convention.

There are few original vocals. Sampled phrases ('get busy, child'), children's records and soundtrack snippets are the lead, which makes the style 'plunderphonics-y'. The Prodigy's Keith Flint on 'Firestarter' is the exception: he wrote his own lines over Howlett's instrumental.
Melody is secondary: a synth line or two fills the holes between samples. The hook is usually a sampled vocal or a riff, such as the Breeders wah guitar looped on 'Firestarter'.

Loudness jumped in the big beat years. In lufs.to's sample the genre's median is -12.4 LUFS; The Prodigy went from -13.6 (Music for the Jilted Generation, 1994) to -8.6 (The Fat of the Land, 1997), and Propellerheads' Decksandrumsandrockandroll (1998) measures -8.5. Breakbeat overall has a median of -13.5.

pitfalls.text: Using a clean, polite break. Big beat breaks are compressed 'liberally' and driven into distortion, so the drums lead the mix instead of sitting behind it.
Setting it at house tempo. The big beat hits sat below house's 120 BPM baseline (Block Rockin' Beats 109, Praise You 110), where a break swings rather than races.
Flagging drums from more than one record in a section as a fault. Here layering breaks from different records is the method: Praise You takes drums from three.

progressions.text: Praise You's intro and verse in Ab Mixolydian: a descending three-chord loop under the Camille Yarbrough vocal.
Right Here Right Now's intro in A Dorian: a thirdless minor tonic against the major IV, the Dorian sixth doing the work.

summary: Dance music built on drum breaks sampled from funk, soul, jazz and R&B records (Amen, Funky Drummer, Apache, Think), rather than on a four-on-the-floor kick. Big beat, its mid-to-late-1990s British peak, compressed and distorted those breaks hard. It sat them between hip-hop and house tempos and layered funk and soul loops, TB-303 acid lines, vocal snippets and rock aggression, arranged with builds, drops and drum rolls.
